text:
Samsung focuses on precision hand, LG highlights versatility in humanoid biz Samsung Electronics and LG Electronics are pursuing markedly different strategies in the robotics market, and the contrast is expected to become more apparent as the two companies showcase their latest technologies and visions at CES 2027.
According to industry officials on Thursday, Samsung Electronics is focusing on precise control of robotic hands and arms, as dexterity is considered one of the most critical capabilities for expanding the practical applications of humanoid robots.
Unlike conventional robots, whose role was repeating a single rigid motion, humanoid robots are required to perform various work in constantly changing real-world environments.
This requires them to go beyond simply grasping and moving objects to handling a wide range of tools and components with precision. The challenge becomes even greater when dealing with delicate and fragile components, which demand increasingly precise control of robotic fingers and arms.
To achieve this, Samsung Electronics' newly established Robotics Experience Division is reportedly focusing on tendon-driven technologies that use actuator-powered cables and pulleys to enable precise control of robotic fingers and joints.
Humanoid robotic hands can be categorized based on their actuation mechanisms. Tesla, for example, employs a tendon-driven system that moves finger joints through cables resembling tendons in the human hand. On the other hand, Boston Dynamics places actuators directly at individual joints.
Tendon-driven systems offer the advantage of lighter fingers, but their cables are subject to wear and require replacement. Joint-level actuation systems, meanwhile, offer precise motion control but face challenges related to motor weight and heat generation.
Samsung Electronics appears to be exploring a tendon-inspired approach that combines motor-driven cables with active and passive pulleys to coordinate finger movements. According to a patent application published in October, the system uses actuators housed in the palm to drive individual fingers, while connected pulleys help coordinate movements across multiple joints.
Last month, Samsung Electronics Executive Chairman Lee Jae-yong visited the Robotics Experience Division at the company's research and development campus in Seoul, where he reportedly reviewed progress in the development of robotic hand technologies.
The company is also conducting research on world models, which predict changes in surrounding environments, and related robot foundation models. Samsung Electronics plans to leverage its network of more than 100 factories and production lines to test robots' ability to perform real-world tasks and further refine their capabilities.
LG Electronics, which first showcased its CLOiD robot in January, is now focusing on its industrial applications. Although CLOiD currently uses a wheeled base, industry officials expect the company to unveil a bipedal humanoid version amid CES 2027.
During its initial showcase at CES 2026 in January, the company positioned CLOiD as a home humanoid robot, demonstrating its ability to perform household chores such as folding laundry and retrieving ingredients. However, LG Electronics is now considering expanding its applications into industrial sites first.
The company recently said it is deploying CLOiD at its washing machine plant in Tennessee to test the robot’s ability to transport washing machine top panels and sort and stack components. LG Electronics is also working with Nvidia to establish a system for collecting approximately 500,000 hours of robot training data by combining real-world and simulated data.
During its third-quarter earnings call, the company said it would “first focus our robotics business on the academic, public and manufacturing sectors, where markets are expected to develop more quickly.”
“As for home robots, we are developing robots and form factors that can naturally integrate into households by leveraging the competitive strengths we have accumulated in the home appliance business.”
“LG Electronics' strength lies in its ability to secure early demand in both the manufacturing and R&D markets,” Daol Securities analyst Kim Yeon-mi said.
“While robotics is not expected to make a meaningful contribution to revenue until around 2030, the company’s key commercialization milestones are scheduled in 2027, making the value of its robotics business more apparent.”
